limit.title: Limit
limit.definition: The limit is the value approached by the outputs as the input approaches a point.
limit.idea: Follow the outputs while the input moves closer to $a$. The value at $a$ can be missing.
limit.example: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=4$, although the quotient is undefined at $2$.

parts.title: Nearby inputs
parts.definition: Approach $a$ through other inputs in the domain.
parts.idea: A hole at $a$ leaves the nearby outputs available.

parts.title: Target value
parts.definition: Outputs eventually lie within any prescribed distance $\varepsilon>0$ of $L$.
parts.idea: A smaller tolerance asks for a closer approximation.
parts.example: A table of $\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ near $2$ suggests a limit of $4$. Factoring gives $x+2$ for $x\ne2$, which proves it.

parts.title: Reading a limit from a graph
parts.definition: The approaching heights determine the one-sided limits. The filled point at the input gives the function value.
parts.idea: Trace the graph toward the input from each side before looking at the filled point.

parts.title: Oscillation
parts.definition: A finite limit cannot exist if inputs arbitrarily near the point keep producing two distinct fixed heights.
parts.idea: Near zero the graph keeps returning to both $1$ and $-1$. A table that samples only one sequence can miss the oscillation.

sides.title: One-sided limits
sides.definition: A one-sided limit restricts the input to one side of the point.
sides.idea: Compare the heights approached by the two branches before declaring a two-sided limit.
sides.example: For $h(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{|x-2|}$, the left limit at $2$ is $-4$ and the right limit is $4$.

parts.title: From the left
parts.definition: Approach $a$ through inputs smaller than $a$.
parts.idea: Choose the branch on the left.

parts.title: From the right
parts.definition: Approach $a$ through inputs larger than $a$.
parts.idea: Choose the branch on the right. The two sides must agree for a finite two-sided limit.

parts.title: Two-sided limit criterion
parts.definition: A finite two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
parts.idea: An open circle can mark the common approaching height even if the function takes a different value at the point.

laws.title: Limit laws
laws.definition: If $f(x)\to L$ and $g(x)\to M$ as $x\to a$, with both limits finite, limit laws combine them by arithmetic wherever the operation is defined.
laws.idea: Once the component limits $L$ and $M$ are known, assemble them in the same order as the expression.

parts.title: Products
parts.definition: The limit of a product is the product of the finite limits.
parts.idea: Treat factors separately, then multiply.

parts.title: Quotients
parts.definition: The quotient law requires a nonzero denominator limit.
parts.idea: Check the denominator before dividing.

parts.title: Constants and linearity
parts.definition: The limit of a constant is that constant. Finite limits commute with sums, differences, and constant multiples.
parts.idea: Start with $\lim_{x\to a}x=a$ and build up a polynomial one term at a time.

parts.title: Powers and roots
parts.definition: Positive integer powers and real roots preserve finite limits on their domains, with a nonnegative radicand for an even root.
parts.idea: Check that the real root is defined along the approach.

squeeze.title: Squeeze theorem
squeeze.definition: A function trapped between two functions with the same limit has that limit.
squeeze.idea: As the gap between the bounds closes, the middle function runs out of room.
squeeze.example: For $x\ne0$, $-x^2\le x^2\sin(1/x)\le x^2$, so the middle expression tends to $0$ as $x\to0$.

parts.title: Bounds
parts.definition: Find a lower and an upper bound near the point.
parts.idea: Bound the oscillating factor by quantities you can control.

parts.title: Common limit
parts.definition: Both bounding functions must approach the same value.
parts.idea: Distinct limiting heights leave a gap.

parts.title: Trigonometric limits
parts.definition: With the angle measured in radians, sine divided by its argument tends to one at zero.
parts.idea: Match the denominator to the angle inside sine. A remaining constant factor stays outside the limit.

continuity.title: Continuity
continuity.definition: A function is continuous at a point in its domain when its limit equals its value there.
continuity.idea: Nearby outputs approach the height of the point actually drawn on the graph.
continuity.example: $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at $0$ even though its graph has a corner there.

parts.title: Point value
parts.definition: Evaluate the function at the specified input.
parts.idea: A filled point gives the actual height.

parts.title: Matching limit
parts.definition: Compare the limiting height with the point value.
parts.idea: A hole or a jump can break the match.

parts.title: One-sided and endpoint continuity
parts.definition: At the left endpoint of a closed interval use the right-hand limit. At the right endpoint use the left-hand limit.
parts.idea: Approach an endpoint through inputs in the interval.

parts.title: Joining two pieces
parts.definition: A piecewise function is continuous at an interior join when both branches approach the assigned value.
parts.idea: Equate the two approaching heights to find an unknown constant, then verify the value at the join.

parts.title: Operations and composition
parts.definition: Sums and products of continuous functions are continuous. Quotients need a nonzero denominator. A composite is continuous when $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ at $g(a)$.
parts.idea: Use the component functions to read off where an expression is continuous. The six trigonometric functions are continuous on their own domains.

ivt.title: Intermediate Value Theorem
ivt.definition: A continuous function on a closed interval attains every value between its endpoint values. Here $m$ and $M$ are the smaller and larger endpoint values.
ivt.idea: A continuous graph going from one height to another passes through each intermediate height $N$.
ivt.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-6x^2+3x-2$, $f(0)=-2$ and $f(2)=12$, so there is a zero in $(0,2)$.

parts.title: Intermediate height
parts.definition: Choose $N$ between the endpoint outputs, in either order.
parts.idea: Pick a horizontal line the graph must meet.

parts.title: A zero
parts.definition: Opposite endpoint signs put height zero strictly between the outputs.
parts.idea: This locates an interval containing a root.

evt.title: Extreme Value Theorem
evt.definition: A continuous function on a closed, bounded interval attains a global minimum and a global maximum. The inputs $u,v$ lie in the interval.
evt.idea: The theorem guarantees that both extreme heights occur. Finding their locations takes another step.

parts.title: Closed interval
parts.definition: The interval includes both endpoints and has finite length.
parts.idea: An omitted endpoint can leave an extreme height unattained.

parts.title: Attainment
parts.definition: Some input realizes each extreme output.
parts.idea: The extrema are values the function actually takes.

endbehavior.title: End behavior and asymptotes
endbehavior.definition: End behavior describes the outputs as inputs grow arbitrarily large in either direction.
endbehavior.idea: Follow the two tails separately. Each may approach a different line.
endbehavior.example: For $f(x)=(x^2-1)/x$, the difference $f(x)-x=-1/x$ tends to $0$ at both ends.

parts.title: Horizontal asymptote
parts.definition: The outputs approach a constant height at the chosen end.
parts.idea: The tail approaches the line $y=L$. The left end uses $x\to-\infty$.

parts.title: Slant asymptote
parts.definition: The vertical distance to a line of nonzero slope tends to zero.
parts.idea: Subtract the proposed line to study the error.

parts.title: Radicals at infinity
parts.definition: Pulling $x^2$ out of a square root produces an absolute value.
parts.idea: Since $|x|/x$ is negative on the left and positive on the right, a radical expression may have two different horizontal asymptotes.

lhospital.title: l’Hospital’s rule
lhospital.definition: For a quotient of form $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$, use the ratio of derivatives when its limit exists. Assume differentiability and $g'\ne0$ in a punctured neighborhood.
lhospital.idea: Relative rates of change can settle which quantity dominates. The same rule applies at infinity.

parts.title: Indeterminate form
parts.definition: Check the separate numerator and denominator limits first.
parts.idea: These symbols name patterns of limits. Neither pattern determines a quotient value.

parts.title: Derivative ratio
parts.definition: Differentiate numerator and denominator separately.
parts.idea: A simpler ratio can have an accessible limit.

derivative.title: Derivative at a point
derivative.definition: The derivative at $a$ is the finite limit of the difference quotient as the input change shrinks to zero.
derivative.idea: Pin one point on the curve and slide a second point toward it. The limiting secant slope is the tangent slope.
derivative.example: For $f(x)=|x|$ at $a=0$, the left-hand slope is $-1$ and the right-hand slope is $1$. The derivative does not exist there.

parts.title: Secant slope
parts.definition: Divide the output change by the input change between two distinct points.
parts.idea: This is the average rate over a nonzero step.
parts.aliases: average rate of change difference quotient

parts.title: Limiting slope
parts.definition: A single finite value must be approached from both sides at an interior point.
parts.idea: Unequal limiting slopes reveal a corner.

derivative2.title: Derivative function
derivative2.definition: The derivative function assigns each input the derivative at that input, wherever it exists.
derivative2.idea: Collect all tangent slopes into a new function.
derivative2.example: For position $s(t)$, the functions $s'(t)$ and $s''(t)$ give velocity and acceleration.

parts.title: At one point
parts.definition: Fix the input and evaluate its slope.
parts.idea: The result is a number.

parts.title: Across inputs
parts.definition: Allow the input to vary.
parts.idea: The graph of the derivative records how the slopes change.

parts.title: Higher-order derivatives
parts.definition: Differentiate again wherever the preceding derivative is differentiable.
parts.idea: Each order measures change in the preceding quantity.

parts.title: Derivative notation
parts.definition: Prime notation and Leibniz notation describe the same derivative when $y=f(x)$.
parts.idea: Leibniz notation makes the variable of differentiation explicit.

parts.title: Differentiability and continuity
parts.definition: A finite derivative at $a$ implies continuity there. Continuity alone does not guarantee a derivative.
parts.idea: At the corner of $y=|x|$, the left and right slopes disagree.

parts.title: Reading the derivative graph
parts.definition: The height of the graph of $f'$ gives the slope of $f$ at the same input. The slope of the graph of $f'$ gives $f''$ where it exists.
parts.idea: Above the axis, the original curve rises. Where the derivative graph itself rises, the original curve bends upward.

tangent.title: Tangent line
tangent.definition: At a differentiable point, the tangent line passes through the point and has slope equal to the derivative.
tangent.idea: The tangent line gives a local linear prediction of the function value.

parts.title: Point of contact
parts.definition: Evaluate the function to locate the point.
parts.idea: This anchors the line to the graph.

parts.title: Tangent slope
parts.definition: Evaluate the derivative at the same input.
parts.idea: This fixes the line's direction.

parts.title: Local linear approximation
parts.definition: Near a differentiability point $a$, the tangent line gives the first-order approximation to the function.
parts.idea: Zoom in at the point of contact. The tangent line predicts the change in height from a small horizontal step.

motion.title: Motion
motion.definition: Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
motion.idea: Position tells where the particle is, velocity tells how it moves, and acceleration tells how its velocity changes.
motion.example: For $s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2$, compare the signs of $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ to decide when the particle speeds up.

parts.title: Speed
parts.definition: Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
parts.idea: Taking the absolute value drops the direction.

parts.title: Speeding up
parts.definition: Away from zero velocity, matching signs of velocity and acceleration increase speed.
parts.idea: A particle speeds up when velocity and acceleration point the same way. Opposite signs mean the particle slows down.

parts.title: Origin, rest, and reversal
parts.definition: Being at the origin means zero position. Rest means zero velocity. Reversal requires a change in the sign of velocity.
parts.idea: Read the event before deciding which equation to solve.

parts.title: Differential equations
parts.definition: A differential equation relates an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives.
parts.idea: For constant mass, a force law describes how position changes by specifying acceleration.

parts.title: Average and instantaneous velocity
parts.definition: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time. Its limit as the time interval shrinks gives instantaneous velocity, when that limit exists.
parts.idea: Two positions determine a secant slope. Bringing the second time closer to the first gives the tangent slope.

rules.title: Differentiation rules
rules.definition: Differentiation rules compute derivatives from the operations used to build a function.
rules.idea: Identify the outermost operation first. A sum, a product, and a composition call for different rules.

parts.title: Product rule
parts.definition: Differentiate each factor in turn and add the two terms.
parts.idea: Each term records the change contributed by one factor.

parts.title: Quotient rule
parts.definition: For $g(x)\ne0$, differentiate the numerator and denominator in the indicated order.
parts.idea: Keep the order in the numerator to obtain the correct sign.

parts.title: Power rule
parts.definition: A power loses one degree on differentiation.
parts.idea: For positive integers $n$, this quickly turns a polynomial into its slope function.

parts.title: Constants and linear combinations
parts.definition: The derivative of a constant is zero. Differentiate sums term by term, carrying along constant factors.
parts.idea: These rules reduce a polynomial to its individual powers.

chain.title: Chain rule
chain.definition: For a differentiable composition, multiply the outer derivative at the inner value by the inner derivative.
chain.idea: A change in the input travels through two functions. Multiply the two rates along that path.

parts.title: Inner change
parts.definition: Differentiate the inside quantity with respect to the original input.
parts.idea: This tells how fast the input to the outer function moves.

parts.title: Outer change
parts.definition: Evaluate the outer derivative at the current inside value.
parts.idea: Combining the two factors gives the rate with respect to $x$.

parts.title: Powers of functions
parts.definition: Differentiate the outer power and multiply by the derivative of the inner function wherever the power rule applies.
parts.idea: In a power of cosine, the power is the outermost operation.

parts.title: Several layers
parts.definition: Each layer of a composition contributes a derivative evaluated at its own input.
parts.idea: Work from the outside inward.

parts.title: Using a table
parts.definition: For $F=f\circ g$, look up the inner value before looking up the outer derivative.
parts.idea: The row for $f'$ is indexed by $g(a)$, which may differ from $a$.

implicit.title: Implicit differentiation
implicit.definition: Implicit differentiation finds the slope of a curve defined by an equation, treating $y$ locally as a differentiable function of $x$.
implicit.idea: An equation can determine the tangent slope even when solving for $y$ is inconvenient.

parts.title: Chain rule for y
parts.definition: Differentiating a power of $y(x)$ introduces its derivative.
parts.idea: The dependent variable changes with $x$.

parts.title: Isolate the slope
parts.definition: Collect terms containing the unknown derivative and solve.
parts.idea: Substituting a point now gives its tangent slope.

parts.title: Vertical tangents
parts.definition: At a regular point of an implicit curve, a vertical tangent occurs when the tangent direction has zero horizontal component.
parts.idea: In the lecture’s curve $x^2+xy+y^2=3$, the slope is $-(2x+y)/(x+2y)$. A zero denominator with a nonzero numerator gives the vertical tangent.

parts.title: Horizontal tangents
parts.definition: At a regular point with a finite slope, the tangent is horizontal exactly when the slope is zero.
parts.idea: Set the numerator of the slope to zero, combine with the curve equation, and verify that the denominator is nonzero.

rates.title: Related rates
rates.definition: Related rates connect time derivatives of quantities constrained by one equation.
rates.idea: A geometric constraint links the changing quantities. Its derivative links their rates at the same instant.

parts.title: Relate quantities
parts.definition: Write an equation valid throughout the motion.
parts.idea: Keep the changing lengths as variables.

parts.title: Relate rates
parts.definition: Differentiate with respect to time before substituting the given instant.
parts.idea: The differentiated constraint reveals the missing rate.

parts.title: Similar triangles
parts.definition: In similar triangles, the ratios of corresponding side lengths are equal.
parts.idea: Multiplying the sides $A,B,C$ by $k$ gives $a,b,c$, respectively. Match corresponding sides before differentiating.

parts.title: Evaluate at the instant
parts.definition: Substitute the stated lengths and rates after differentiating the relation in time.
parts.idea: A length known at one instant may still be changing. Early substitution loses its rate.

inverse.title: Inverse functions
inverse.definition: An inverse function reverses a one-to-one function on its range.
inverse.idea: Exchanging input and output exchanges horizontal and vertical changes, giving reciprocal slopes where the original slope is nonzero.
inverse.example: If $f(2)=5$ and $f'(2)=-3$, the inverse derivative at $5$ is $-1/3$ under the inverse derivative theorem's hypotheses.

parts.title: Corresponding points
parts.definition: An output of the original function becomes an input of its inverse.
parts.idea: Keep track of which input belongs to each function.

parts.title: Reciprocal slope
parts.definition: If $f$ is continuous and one-to-one on an open interval, differentiable at $a$, and $f'(a)\ne0$, its inverse is differentiable at $b=f(a)$.
parts.idea: The slope at $b$ uses the original derivative at $a$.

parts.title: One-to-one and domain restrictions
parts.definition: A function is one-to-one when equal outputs force equal inputs.
parts.idea: Each horizontal line meets the graph at most once. Restricting $x^2$ to $x\ge0$ gives the inverse $\sqrt{x}$.

exp.title: Exponentials and logarithms
exp.definition: The natural exponential has derivative equal to itself. The natural logarithm is its inverse on positive inputs.
exp.idea: Exponential growth is proportional to the amount present. Its inverse translates multiplicative change into addition.

parts.title: General base
parts.definition: A positive constant base contributes a logarithmic factor.
parts.idea: Writing $a^x=e^{x\ln a}$ explains the factor.

parts.title: Log of a function
parts.definition: Apply the chain rule where the inside is positive.
parts.idea: This expresses the derivative relative to the current value.

parts.title: The number e
parts.definition: The natural base is the base whose exponential has slope one at $(0,1)$.
parts.idea: Every exponential $a^x$ passes through $(0,1)$. Its slope there determines the constant in its derivative.

parts.title: Relative growth
parts.definition: For positive $y$, relative growth is the instantaneous rate divided by the current value.
parts.idea: An exponential has constant relative growth.

parts.title: Logarithms in other bases
parts.definition: For $a>0$, $a\ne1$, and $x>0$, change of base gives the derivative of $\log_a x$.
parts.idea: Dividing $\ln x$ by the constant $\ln a$ changes the scale.

parts.title: Logarithm laws
parts.definition: For positive inputs, logarithms turn products into sums, quotients into differences, and powers into multiples.
parts.idea: Break a complicated product into terms before differentiating.

logdiff.title: Logarithmic differentiation
logdiff.definition: Logarithmic differentiation takes the logarithm of a positive function, differentiates implicitly, and solves for its derivative.
logdiff.idea: A logarithm turns products into sums and brings a variable exponent down where it can be differentiated.

parts.title: Bring down the exponent
parts.definition: For a positive base, take logarithms on both sides.
parts.idea: A variable power becomes a product.

parts.title: Recover the derivative
parts.definition: Multiply the differentiated identity by the original function.
parts.idea: Substitute the original expression for $y$ at the end.

parts.title: Real exponents
parts.definition: For any real constant $r$, the power rule holds for $x>0$.
parts.idea: Write $\ln y=r\ln x$ and differentiate.

parts.title: Variable base and exponent
parts.definition: If $u$ and $v$ are differentiable and $u>0$, logarithmic differentiation separates their contributions to the derivative of $y=u^v$.
parts.idea: Changing the exponent contributes the logarithm term. Changing the base contributes the relative rate of the base. Multiply by $y$ to recover the derivative.

trig.title: Trigonometric derivatives
trig.definition: With angles measured in radians, sine differentiates to cosine and cosine to negative sine.
trig.idea: The unit circle connects the rate of change of one coordinate to the other coordinate.

parts.title: Fundamental limit
parts.definition: Near zero the sine of a radian angle is approximately the angle itself.
parts.idea: This supplies the scale in the derivative of sine.

parts.title: An inside angle
parts.definition: A varying angle contributes its own rate by the chain rule.
parts.idea: A faster-moving angle changes the output faster.

parts.title: Tangent and cotangent
parts.definition: On their domains, the derivative of tangent is secant squared and the derivative of cotangent is negative cosecant squared.
parts.idea: Write each function as a quotient of sine and cosine to recover the sign.

parts.title: Secant and cosecant
parts.definition: Differentiate each reciprocal on its domain.
parts.formula:
$(\sec x)'=\sec x\tan x$
$(\csc x)'=-\csc x\cot x$
parts.idea: Express secant as the reciprocal of cosine and cosecant as the reciprocal of sine.

derivatives.title: Second derivative
derivatives.definition: The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative, wherever it exists.
derivatives.idea: The first derivative gives the slope. The second tells how rapidly that slope changes as the input moves.

parts.title: Slope changing
parts.definition: Take the rate of change of the tangent slope.
parts.idea: A locally constant slope gives zero second derivative.

parts.title: Stationary point test
parts.definition: At a stationary point with continuous second derivative nearby, its sign can classify the point.
parts.idea: Positive second derivative bends the graph upward at its horizontal tangent.

monotonic.title: Increasing and decreasing
monotonic.definition: A function increases on an interval when larger inputs always give larger outputs there. For a decreasing function, the output order reverses.
monotonic.idea: Compare two inputs to define increase. The sign of the derivative lets you detect it across an interval.
monotonic.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-12x+12$, $f'$ is positive to the left of $-1$, negative between $-1$ and $1$, and positive to the right of $1$.

parts.title: Increasing
parts.definition: Positive derivative throughout an interval ensures increase there.
parts.idea: The Mean Value Theorem connects tangent slopes to the change between any two inputs.

parts.title: Decreasing
parts.definition: Negative derivative throughout an interval ensures decrease there.
parts.idea: Each secant across the interval then slopes downward.

parts.title: Mean Value Theorem
parts.definition: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, some $c$ strictly between $a$ and $b$ has slope equal to the secant slope.
parts.idea: Apply the theorem between any two inputs. If the derivative is positive throughout the interval, the second output must be larger.

concavity.title: Concavity
concavity.definition: On an interval, a differentiable graph is concave up when its tangent slopes increase and concave down when they decrease. In the formulas, $u<v$ are any two inputs in the interval.
concavity.idea: A line keeps the same slope. Concavity describes which way a curve bends away from its tangent as its slope changes.
concavity.example: For $g(x)=x^3+1$, $g''(x)=6x$. The graph is concave down to the left of $0$ and concave up to the right.

parts.title: Concave up
parts.definition: Tangent slopes increase as the input moves right.
parts.idea: Even a falling curve can bend upward as its slopes become less negative.

parts.title: Concave down
parts.definition: Tangent slopes decrease as the input moves right.
parts.idea: Even a rising curve can bend downward as its slopes become less positive.

parts.title: Tangent comparison
parts.definition: On a concave-up interval the graph lies on or above each tangent line. For concave down, the inequality reverses.
parts.idea: Comparing the curve with its linear prediction makes the bend visible.

inflect.title: Inflection points
inflect.definition: An inflection point is a point of continuity where the graph changes concavity. One way to verify this is a sign change of the second derivative.
inflect.idea: Look on both sides of the point to see whether the direction of bending switches.
inflect.example: For $g(x)=x^3+1$, $g''(x)=6x$ changes sign at $0$, so $(0,1)$ is an inflection point.

parts.title: Candidate
parts.definition: An interior input where the second derivative vanishes or fails to exist is worth checking.
parts.idea: The candidate still needs a change in concavity.

parts.title: Change of sign
parts.definition: Opposite signs of the second derivative on the two sides establish opposite concavities.
parts.idea: A sign chart records the behavior on intervals around the input.

critical.title: Critical numbers
critical.definition: A critical number is an input in the domain where the derivative is zero or fails to exist.
critical.idea: Critical numbers narrow the search for interior extrema. Check what the function does on either side.
critical.example: For $f(x)=x^3$, $f'(0)=0$ and the graph increases through $0$.

parts.title: Stationary input
parts.definition: The derivative exists and equals zero.
parts.idea: A horizontal tangent marks an input to investigate.

parts.title: Undefined derivative
parts.definition: The point belongs to the graph even though its derivative fails to exist.
parts.idea: A corner can be an extremum, as with $|x|$ at zero.

parts.title: Critical value
parts.definition: A critical number is an input $c$. Its corresponding output is called a critical value.
parts.idea: The derivative locates candidate inputs. Compare the function values to decide which one is highest or lowest.

global.title: Global extrema
global.definition: A global maximum or minimum is an output at least as large or as small as every output on the entire domain $D$.
global.idea: The comparison includes every feasible input. An endpoint can win.
global.example: For $f(x)=x+2$ on $[-1,1]$, the minimum is $1$ and the maximum is $3$.

parts.title: Global maximum
parts.definition: At a maximizing input, every domain value is at most its output.
parts.idea: Compare heights across the entire graph.

parts.title: Global minimum
parts.definition: At a minimizing input, every domain value is at least its output.
parts.idea: On a closed interval, include both endpoints among the candidates.

parts.title: Closed-interval method
parts.definition: For a continuous function on $[a,b]$, compare its values at the endpoints and at every interior critical number.
parts.idea: The largest candidate value is the global maximum. The smallest is the global minimum.

local.title: Local extrema
local.definition: A local extremum is an output that is largest or smallest among outputs sufficiently near its input. In both inequalities, $x$ ranges over nearby inputs in the domain.
local.formula:
$\text{Local maximum:}\quad f(x)\le f(c)$
$\text{Local minimum:}\quad f(x)\ge f(c)$
local.idea: Look a short distance to the left and right. A change from rising to falling produces a peak.
local.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-12x+12$, $f(-1)=20$ is a local maximum and $f(1)=4$ is a local minimum.

parts.title: Local maximum
parts.definition: The output is at least as large as all nearby domain values.
parts.idea: A change in the sign of $f'$ from positive to negative produces this shape at a continuous interior point.

parts.title: Local minimum
parts.definition: The output is at most as large as all nearby domain values.
parts.idea: A change in the sign of $f'$ from negative to positive produces a valley at a continuous interior point.

optimization.title: Optimization
optimization.definition: Optimization finds the largest or smallest value of an objective subject to constraints.
optimization.idea: The objective says what counts as best. The constraints determine which choices are possible.
optimization.example: For $x,y\ge0$ and $x+y=6$, the product $xy$ has maximum $9$ at $(3,3)$.

parts.title: Objective
parts.definition: Write the quantity to maximize or minimize as a function.
parts.idea: This is the number used to compare feasible choices.

parts.title: Constraint
parts.definition: Use the relation and domain restrictions to reduce the variables.
parts.idea: Now compare $P(x)=x(6-x)$ at the endpoints and interior critical numbers.

parts.title: Feasible inputs
parts.definition: The feasible domain consists of all inputs allowed by the constraints and the model.
parts.idea: Reduce the objective to one variable, then check candidates and included endpoints. On an open end, examine what the objective approaches.

parts.title: Gradient descent
parts.definition: In one variable, a descent step moves against the derivative of a loss $L$, with a small positive step size $\eta$.
parts.idea: A positive slope points uphill to the right, so the step moves left. The valley reached can depend on the starting point.

sketch.title: Curve sketching
sketch.definition: Curve sketching combines the domain, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes, extrema and concavity to draw a graph.
sketch.idea: Function values place the graph. Derivative signs tell how to connect those points and how each piece bends.
sketch.example: For $f(x)=x/(x+1)$, the domain excludes $-1$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=1$.

parts.title: First derivative chart
parts.definition: Split the domain into intervals and record the sign of the derivative.
parts.idea: This gives the direction of motion along each branch.

parts.title: Second derivative chart
parts.definition: On each interval where its sign is fixed, the second derivative gives the direction of bending.
parts.idea: Use this with the first chart to draw the shape of each branch.

parts.title: Domain and intercepts
parts.definition: An $x$-intercept has zero output. The $y$-intercept is the value at zero if zero lies in the domain.
parts.idea: Mark holes and breaks first. A zero of a canceled expression can be outside the original domain.

parts.title: Symmetry and periodicity
parts.definition: Even and odd symmetry require a domain symmetric about zero. A period $T>0$ must preserve the domain under translation.
parts.idea: Reflection, rotation through the origin, or repetition can determine a whole branch from one piece.

parts.title: Assembling the sketch
parts.definition: Determine the domain, intercepts, symmetry, and asymptotes. Then mark increase and decrease, local extrema, concavity, and inflection points before drawing each branch.
parts.idea: Plot the points and asymptotes first. The two derivative sign charts constrain how to join them.

parts.title: Holes in a sketch
parts.definition: At an excluded input with a finite two-sided limit, place an open circle at the limiting height.
parts.idea: Use the simplified formula to find the height, then return to the original domain to decide whether the point is included.

functions.title: Functions and domains
functions.definition: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain $D$. Its range is the set of outputs attained.
functions.idea: Start by asking which inputs are allowed. A formula and a domain together determine the function.
functions.example: The tank model $W(t)=6+3t$ has domain $[0,4]$ minutes and range $[6,18]$ liters.

parts.title: Composition
parts.definition: A composite feeds the output of $g$ into $f$. An input must lie in the domain of $g$ and its output in the domain of $f$.
parts.idea: Read from the inside out. Reversing the order can change both the rule and the domain.

parts.title: Piecewise functions
parts.definition: A piecewise definition assigns different formulas on specified parts of a domain.
parts.idea: At a boundary, the inequality tells you which piece supplies the value.

parts.title: Real domains and exclusions
parts.definition: A denominator must be nonzero, and a real even root requires a nonnegative radicand.
parts.idea: Record restrictions before simplifying. Canceling a factor leaves its original excluded inputs excluded.

unitcircle.title: Radians and the unit circle
unitcircle.definition: An angle of $\theta$ radians cuts off a signed arc of length $r\theta$ on a circle of radius $r$.
unitcircle.idea: On the unit circle, angles measure distance traveled around the circle. The horizontal and vertical coordinates give cosine and sine.

parts.title: Unit-circle coordinates
parts.definition: An angle measured counterclockwise from the positive horizontal axis ends at the point with coordinates cosine and sine.
parts.idea: The quadrant gives each sign, and the reference triangle gives each magnitude.

parts.title: Amplitude and period
parts.definition: For $y=A\sin x$ with $A\ne0$, the amplitude is the distance from the midline to a peak. The period is the length of one cycle.
parts.idea: Multiplying sine by three triples the height and leaves a full cycle the same length.

infinite.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
infinite.definition: An infinite limit at $a$ means the outputs eventually exceed every positive bound, or fall below every negative bound, as inputs approach $a$.
infinite.idea: The input approaches a finite number. Trace each branch separately to see which way the output goes.
infinite.example: For $f(x)=-2/(x-1)^3$, the left branch rises without bound and the right branch falls without bound at $x=1$.

parts.title: Vertical asymptote
parts.definition: The line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote if at least one one-sided limit there is infinite.
parts.idea: A single unbounded branch is enough.

parts.title: Odd and even powers
parts.definition: Near zero, an odd power of the displacement changes sign across the point. An even power stays positive on both sides.
parts.idea: For $1/x$ the branches point in opposite directions. For $1/x^2$ both branches rise.

limitmethods.title: Algebraic limit methods
limitmethods.definition: Two expressions that agree on a punctured neighborhood of $a$ have the same limit there, whenever either limit exists.
limitmethods.idea: Substitution tells you what to try next. If it gives zero over zero, simplify the expression for nearby inputs.

parts.title: Direct substitution
parts.definition: A polynomial can be evaluated directly at the limiting input. A rational function also allows substitution wherever its denominator is nonzero.
parts.idea: Check the denominator before using the quotient law.

parts.title: Factoring and cancellation
parts.definition: A factor that is nonzero near $a$ may be canceled when evaluating a limit there.
parts.idea: The simplified expression agrees at every nearby input that the limit uses.

parts.title: Conjugates
parts.definition: Multiplying by a conjugate converts a difference of square roots into a difference of radicands.
parts.idea: The new numerator may have a common factor with the denominator.
parts.example: For the limit at $x=5$, multiplying by $\sqrt{x+4}+3$ reduces the quotient to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+3}$, whose limit is $\frac16$.

parts.title: Nonzero over zero
parts.definition: If the numerator tends to a nonzero number and the denominator tends to zero, the magnitude of the quotient grows without bound.
parts.idea: Check the signs on each side to decide which branch rises and which falls.

breaks.title: Discontinuities
breaks.definition: A function is discontinuous at $a$ if its value is missing, its finite limit fails to exist, or the two values differ.
breaks.idea: Compare the two approaching heights, then check the point itself. These three observations distinguish holes, jumps, and vertical asymptotes.
breaks.example: Changing one point can fill a hole. It cannot join two branches that approach different heights.

parts.title: Removable discontinuity
parts.definition: The finite two-sided limit $L$ exists, but the function value is missing or differs from $L$.
parts.idea: Assigning $f(a)=L$ fills the hole.
parts.example: On a sketch, mark a hole with an open circle. The original domain determines whether that input belongs to the graph.

parts.title: Jump discontinuity
parts.definition: Both one-sided limits are finite and have different values.
parts.idea: Each branch reaches a definite height. Changing the point cannot make those heights match.

parts.title: Infinite discontinuity
parts.definition: At least one branch is unbounded in the sense of an infinite one-sided limit.
parts.idea: A vertical asymptote locates the break. The left branch may behave differently.

invtrig.title: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
invtrig.definition: An inverse trigonometric function returns the angle on a chosen branch with the specified trigonometric value. For arcsine the returned angle lies in $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
invtrig.idea: Choose a branch where each output corresponds to one angle. The slope of the inverse is the reciprocal slope at that angle whenever the original slope is nonzero.
invtrig.example: In the lecture, differentiating $\arctan\sqrt{x}$ uses the inverse tangent derivative and the chain rule.

parts.title: Arcsine and arccosine
parts.definition: For $|x|<1$, the two slopes have the same magnitude and opposite signs.
parts.idea: On their principal branches, sine increases and cosine decreases.
parts.aliases: arcsin arccos inverse sine inverse cosine
parts.example: For $y=\arcsin x$, differentiate $\sin y=x$ to get $\cos y\,y'=1$. On the chosen branch, $\cos y=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.

parts.title: Arctangent and arccotangent
parts.definition: Both derivatives exist for every real input on the branches used in lecture.
parts.idea: The identity $1+\tan^2y=\sec^2y$ expresses the reciprocal slope using the input.
parts.aliases: arctan arccot inverse tangent inverse cotangent

parts.title: Arcsecant and arccosecant
parts.definition: Both derivatives require $|x|>1$.
parts.idea: The absolute value keeps the denominator positive on both branches.
parts.aliases: arcsec arccsc inverse secant inverse cosecant

tests.title: Tests for local extrema
tests.definition: Derivative tests classify local extrema by a change in direction or, at a stationary point, by concavity.
tests.idea: A critical number gives a place to check. To classify it, examine what the graph does on either side.
tests.example: For $f(x)=x^3$, the origin is stationary. The derivative stays positive on both sides, so the graph keeps rising.

parts.title: Fermat’s theorem
parts.definition: At an interior local extremum where $f$ is differentiable, its derivative is zero.
parts.idea: A smooth peak or valley has a horizontal tangent. Corners and included endpoints must also be checked.

parts.title: First derivative test
parts.definition: At an interior critical number where $f$ is continuous, a change in the sign of $f'$ determines the extremum.
parts.idea: Read the sign chart left to right. If the sign stays the same on both sides, the graph keeps moving in the same direction.
parts.example: For $f(x)=4x^3-12x+12$, the sign of $f'$ changes from positive to negative at $-1$, giving a local maximum of $f(-1)=20$.

parts.title: Second derivative test
parts.definition: If $f'(c)=0$, a positive second derivative gives a local minimum and a negative one gives a local maximum.
parts.idea: If $f''(c)=0$, use another test. At zero the functions $x^4$ and $x^3$ both have vanishing first and second derivatives, but only the first has a minimum.

rationaltails.title: End behavior of rational functions
rationaltails.definition: At either infinite end, a nonzero rational function behaves like the ratio of its leading terms. Here $a_m,b_n$ are the leading coefficients.
rationaltails.idea: Compare the degrees first. When the numerator has degree one higher, division gives the equation of the slant line.
rationaltails.example: Dividing $x^2$ by $x-1$ gives $x+1+\frac{1}{x-1}$. The graph approaches $y=x+1$ at both ends.

parts.title: Degree comparison
parts.definition: Let $m$ and $n$ be the numerator and denominator degrees. For $m<n$ the ratio tends to zero. For $m=n$ it tends to the ratio of leading coefficients.
parts.idea: If $m>n$, the magnitude grows without bound. Use the leading coefficient ratio and the parity of $m-n$ to find the sign at each end.

parts.title: Polynomial division
parts.definition: Divide the numerator by the denominator to get a quotient $S$ and a remainder $R$ of lower degree than $Q$.
parts.idea: The remainder term tends to zero at either infinite end. When $S$ is linear with nonzero slope, its graph is a slant asymptote.

forms.title: Rewriting indeterminate forms
forms.definition: An indeterminate form gives too little information to determine a limit from the separate limits of its factors or terms.
forms.idea: Rewrite the expression as a quotient. For a positive base raised to a variable exponent, first take the logarithm.
forms.example: In $\lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x$, rewrite the product as $\frac{\ln x}{1/x}$ to apply l’Hospital’s rule.

parts.title: Products
parts.definition: A product with one factor tending to zero and the other unbounded can be rewritten as a quotient.
parts.idea: At $0^+$ the rewritten quotient has the form required by l’Hospital’s rule.

parts.title: Differences
parts.definition: An indeterminate difference of unbounded terms may become a quotient after taking a common denominator or rationalizing.
parts.idea: At $0^+$ the combined expression has form zero over zero.

parts.title: Indeterminate powers
parts.definition: For a positive base, take the logarithm to turn a variable power into a product.
parts.idea: Find the limit of the logarithm, then exponentiate. For $(1+x)^{1/x}$ at $0^+$, the logarithm tends to one and the original power tends to $e$.
